replying_to: Replying to Unsupervised Contrastive Learning for Signal-Dependent Noise Synthesis
display_title: Official Review of Paper4467 by Reviewer a4bS

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper constructs a neural model for synthesizing noise in images. The model is based on a generic pretext task instead of real noise measured from images, or analysis of processes that generate noise in real world. The paper claims that the resulting noise is realistic but gives no convincing theoretical or experimental support to that statement.
content.main_review:
The premise of the paper is puzzling. The used pretext task essentially only requires the noise to be somehow dependent on the image, and further regularization terms later enforce, e.g., the desired magnitude for the noise. This approach would make sense if there were only one way for noise to be signal-dependent, and if this were the case the method should find it. But this is obviously not true.

The paper claims that the noise “shows advantages over the noise synthesized by traditional statistical models both qualitatively and quantitatively” but shows neither.

First, the images in the paper are somehow incorrect, apparently having been compressed or resampled so that their frequency profile has changed considerably. The AWGN images show spurious correlations such as disproportional amount of horizontal and vertical features and splotchy coloration. I double-checked this by adding various amounts of Gaussian noise to the top image in Figure 1(a) and could not reach anything that looked like the image in column 1(b). Figure 1(b) simply looks wrong, as do all other purported instances of AWGN in the paper. Given this discrepancy, I cannot place any trust on the arguments based on visual comparisons. This includes the mention in Section 4.2 about the preferences of external viewers. To be convincing, a perceptual test would require a thorough description of test protocol and results in any case.

In Section 4.2, the paper argues that statistical noise models have several weaknesses by design that CoNo could in theory avoid thanks to its Glow-based design. However, there is no attempt to explain why CoNo still wouldn’t have those weaknesses, or any number of new ones, given that its training is not based on data on realistic noise but just the oversimplified pretext task and regularization terms. The training does not consider how noise is formed in a digital camera pipeline, in analog photography, or in the visual system of a biological observer. Still, CoNo is purportedly more realistic than previous models that attempt to mimic these processes. This doesn’t make any sense to me.

After reading the paper, my theory is that the properties of the noise synthesized by CoNo arise solely from the inductive biases of the Glow model used. If these inductive biases happen to be beneficial for, e.g., data augmentation for training classifiers, that would be an interesting result, but the extremely terse quantitative evaluation in Section 4.3 is not convincing in this regard.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper builds on the premise that a simple pretext task and some regularization will result in the generation of realistic, signal-dependent noise after unsupervised training of a neural noise model. Without any consideration to how noise is formed in real-world processes, or training data from which this could be learned, the idea could only work if there was just one possible way to generate noise that fulfills the pretext task. As this is not true, the paper is chasing an impossible goal, and the properties of the generated noise, or its usefulness in any application, remain unknown and unproven.

content.title: Unconvinced Comments with Misunderstandings
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time, feedback, and concrete comments that improve the quality of our work. Especially, the authors want to thank the encouraging comments from all reviewers, e.g. "**first work that uses UCL for noise synthesis**" [yC7E], "**novel**" [yC7E, SqsX ], "**well-written and easy to read**" [SqsX], and "**well incorporates the idea of contrastive learning into the noise synthesis problem**" [SqsX].

We regret that you find nothing interesting or insightful from this study. However, the authors believe that there are misunderstandings and factual errors. 

**Q**: *"The model is based on a generic pretext task instead of real noise measured from images, or analysis of processes that generate noise in real world."*  
**A**: We politely emphasize that the main contribution of this work is to present **an alternative noise synthesis framework to traditional statistical models**, where **only clean images are available**. So, measuring or understanding real noise is not the purpose of this study and is not applicable under our problem formulation.

**Q**: *"The premise of the paper is puzzling. This approach would make sense if there were only one way for noise to be signal-dependent."*  
**A**: We respectfully disagree with the comments. The proposed method is an alternative to statistical models such as NLF, which is commonly adopted as the synthetic noise model. That is to say, the proposed method should **work wherever the statistical models can be applied**. Note, in this work, the problem setting has only clean images.

**Q**: *"The images in the paper are somehow incorrect."* and qualitative comparison.  
**A**: The authors assume that the images in this work are genuine. The reviewer mentions that *"I double-checked this by adding various amounts of Gaussian noise to the top image in Figure 1(a)"*. We politely emphasize that **the noise is generated in the RAW domain**. This is shown in Fig. 2 and described in Sec. 4.1 Implementation.  We follow the same implementation in [1]. **Adding noise directly in the RGB domain is not an appropriate reimplementation**, and will lead to an unfair assessment and biased conclusion.

[1] Abdelhamed et al., Noise flow: Noise modeling with conditional normalizing flows. ICCV 2019

**Q**: *"there is no attempt to explain why CoNo still wouldn’t have those weaknesses"*  and *"but just the oversimplified pretext task and regularization terms"*.  
**A**:  We respectfully disagree with the comments. First, in Sec. 4.2 Noise Synthesis of the initial version, we have stated *"These non-photon noise can not be easily modeled via statistical models. Moreover, statistical models such as AWGN and NLF tend to assume independence between the pixels. As a comparison, CoNo does not have this inductive bias. Meanwhile, the convolution operations give
CoNo more flexibility in synthesizing the signal-dependent noise."* Second, one of the contributions of this work is to show a simple pretext task can lead to better performance than statistical models. 

**Q**: *"Still, CoNo is purportedly more realistic than previous models that attempt to mimic these processes."*  
**A**: We **never** claim that the proposed method outperforms previous models that mimic digital or biological processes. The empirical results only show that CoNo outperforms traditional models (AWGN, NLF) by generating more realistic noise. This is aligned with our major claim. Again, the core idea of this paper is to **present a novel data-driven approach alternative to traditional statistical models**.

**Q**: *"the properties of the noise synthesized by CoNo arise solely from the inductive biases of the Glow model used"*.  
**A**: We partially agree that Glow-based model plays an important role in noise synthesis. However, we politely emphasize that a standalone Glow model does not work. The main challenge is how to transform plain Gaussian noise into signal-dependent noise. We want to highlight that the technical contributions include **instance-wise discrimination task**, **MMD-based contrastive loss**, and **signal-dependent fusion layer**, with the help of perceptual and moment-matching regularization. Especially, we are the first to design such an instance-wise discrimination task for the noise synthesis.

Sincerely, we hope the technical contributions could be re-assessed based on the replies above.

content.title: Clarification of position
content.comment:
Thank you for the reply. I indeed did not notice that the noise was added in RAW domain, and that would explain why it looks different than I expected. However, this also means that the demosaicing pipeline may have a significant effect on the properties of the final RGB pixel values, and this is not analyzed in the paper.

The paper was very clear about offering an alternative method for noise synthesis, and I did not miss that. My point was that the paper contains no justification as to why the noise synthesized in this alternative way would have any particular properties or be useful in any particular task.

I do not think that the added Figure 5 helps the situation. It appears that CoNo produces somewhat larger variation for brighter pixels, but that would happen even if networks $a(\mathbf{x})$ and $b(\mathbf{x})$ in Eq. 11 had constant outputs, as the noise magnitude is scaled by the clean input $\mathbf{x}$ in Eq. 11. Completely removing dependency on $\mathbf{x}$ would require $\mathbf{A}\approx0$, i.e., $a(\mathbf{x})\approx-\infty$ in Eq. 11, and I do not find it surprising that this does not happen, given that there is no pressure to remove this dependency. Elaborating a bit further, with $\mathbf{A}=\mathit{const.}$ and $\mathbf{B} \approx 0$, Eq. 11 would be a reasonable approximation of Poisson photon noise. With $\mathbf{A} \approx 0$ and $\mathbf{B}=\mathit{const.}$, Eq. 11 produces AWGN. Other values for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ produce some mixture of them, but the end result is always modulated Gaussian noise.

Reiterating my main point of criticism, nothing in the training process or the model being trained does, in my view, motivate why the networks $a(\mathbf{x})$ and $b(\mathbf{x})$ would learn to perform any particular function. It follows that there is no reason for the generated noise to have any particular properties. To fulfill the pretext task and the regularization terms, there must be an enormously wide choice for functions $a$ and $b$, and each choice comes with different properties for the generated noise. In fact, we could probably just choose two constants $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x})=A$ and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})=B$ that result in the desired average noise amplitude, and I cannot see why that would not fulfill the pretext task just as well as the learned networks. The paper does not discuss or even acknowledge this apparent ill-posedness of the task at all, and neither do the authors' replies to the reviews.

I also cannot quite agree that the empirical results "show that CoNo outperforms traditional models (AWGN, NLF) by generating more realistic noise" as claimed in the rebuttal. The denoising results of the proxy task in Table 1 are low compared to the current state of the art where up to 10 dB better results have been obtained, so the validity of the proxy task is questionable. Using $L_1$ loss for training the denoisers is an especially strange choice, given that maximizing PSNR is equivalent to minimizing $L_2$ loss, not $L_1$. Also, AWGN is understandably a bad model for the real-world noise in DND and SIDD datasets, but how well were the parameters for NLF chosen? There are many ways to get the same overall $\sigma$ with different choices for $\lambda_\mathrm{shot}$ and $\lambda_\mathrm{read}$ (Eq. 3), and it is critical how well these match the data to be denoised. The paper offers no details of this.

It would have been much more convincing if the paper used DND and SIDD datasets to provide direct, large-scale, quantitative comparisons of the generated noise vs real noise, e.g., using signal level dependent noise magnitude histograms. And I do not quite follow the objection that the purpose is not for the noise to be realistic, given that the paper says that "we conclude that CoNo can synthesize more realistic noise than AWGN and NLF", and even the rebuttal states that CoNo outperforms traditional models "by generating more realistic noise".

In summary, I do not think it is enough to show an alternative way to do something. The important part is showing that the alternative way is somehow useful and superior to existing methods, or, in a pinch, at least has interesting properties (in this case, those properties would need to be very carefully analyzed). I do not think the submission is at all sufficient in these regards.

content.title: Clarifications on Divergences and Misunderstandings
content.comment:
Thank you for your reply. We admire your honesty in admitting the factual error in the first-round review, as it takes real courage to do so. 

Though most comments (except the new Fig. 5) should appear in the first round review, the authors are glad to see that there are more technical feedbacks in the second round. As the second round comment comes after the Discussion Stage, the purpose of our reply is sorely to further clarify the divergences and misunderstandings, instead of revising the paper.

First, **the fundamental divergence between the reviewer and authors seems to be the perception of the paper's contribution**. The authors aim to present a novel application/adaptation of SSL/UCL at a learning conference. However, the SSL part, which is the core contribution of this work, seems to be ignored as there is no positive/negative comment on the SSL part.

The second divergence is the perception of *"more realistic than traditional statistical models"*. The authors make this claim based on the fact that rigid statistical models can only model the photon noise with a linear relationship, ignoring the non-linearity and non-photon noise. Note, the proposed method design a pretext task based on empirical observation (Asm. 1) for a Glow-based model, which introduces both non-linearity and flexibility. Thus, theoretically, CoNo shows advantages over statistical models as it does not have linear inductive bias. While visual comparison might be subjective, we use a proxy evaluation protocol to justify this. **We respectfully disagree with the claim that no justification is provided.** The intuition is that a smaller distributional divergence between the source domain and the target domain leads to a smaller performance gap. This is inspired by unsupervised domain adaptation. Of course, we understand that the reviewer has a different opinion on "realistic" as an adjective could be subjective.

The third divergence is the preception of SSL. Here, the proposed framework is based on end-to-end learning, as the whole training process is modulated by the pretext task and the regularization term. We appreciate that the reviewer has some interesting extreme case analysis on the effect **A(x)** and **B(x)**. However, these are inconclusive as the signal-dependent fusion layer is trained jointly with the Glow-based model, there are both convolution and channel-wise interactions. We understand that the reviewer tends to have a step-by-step analysis. However, this is not feasible for our case.
Again, we gently remind the reviewer that the contribution of this work is how to learn parameters, including **A** and **B** in an unsupervised fashion, which is drastically different from statistical models.

For your specific questions:

**Q**: *the demosaicing pipeline may have a significant effect on the properties of the final RGB pixel values*    
**A**: We partially agree with this. We use a simple linear demosaicing following (Abdelhamed et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2020) for all models, which should be. Note, the focus of the paper is SSL, not image processing. The effect of demosaicing could be an interesting ablation for future work.

**Q**: *no justification*   
**A**: Since this is the only concern we met about no justification, we clarify this in the second divergence above. 

**Q**: analysis on **A** and **B**    
**A**: We partly address your question above. There are an enormous number of choices for **A** and **B**. The question is how to learn it. The paper proposes a reasonable solution based on Asm. 1. Both qualitative and quantitative results suggest that CoNo is a doable solution. We respectfully disagree

**Q**: *low compared to the current state of the art*    
**A**: Note, we adopt a proxy evaluation protocol, the denoising is not the goal of this work. We only have a simple experimental setup with a plain DnCNN. Comparing with SOTA is neither reasonable nor fair for this experiment.

**Q**: *direct, large-scale, quantitative comparisons*    
**A**: We politely emphasize that the problem formulation is that only clean RGB images are available. The suggested experiment is not feasible. Thus we only compare with traditional statistical models. Also, it is neither professional nor reasonable to ask for large-scale experiments after the Discussion Period, as is impractical for the authors to revise the paper.

**Q**: *the parameters for NLF*  
**A**: Please check the appendix in the original submission.

**Q**: *at least has interesting properties*  
**A**: CoNo has at least two properties superior to statistical models, 1) non-linearity (e.g. in Fig. 5) and 2) the flexibility to model non-photon noise endowed by Glow. Statistical models do not have such non-linearity, and we enable the use of Glow via SSL.

Though it is difficult to clear all divergences, the authors sincerely expect the reply can help future readers better understand the contribution.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an unsupervised noise synthesis framework, Contrastive Noise (CoNo). CoNo uses MMD as a distance metric in contrastive learning. It also utilizes consistency (i.e., perceptual) and distributional alignment losses specialized in this noise synthesis problem. This paper verifies the effectiveness of CoNo by comparing CoNo with popular statistical noises, AWGN and NLF.
content.main_review:
### Strengths
S1. This paper well adapts contrastive learning to the noise synthesis problem. \
S2. This paper is generally well-written, so it is easy to read. \
S3. The intuition of the proposed method (Assumption 1) is clear, so I think the method is reasonable and well-designed.

---
### Weaknesses and Questions
W1. Why MMD instead of cosine distance?
- This paper uses MMD as a distance metric instead of the cosine distance. However, I cannot find why MMD should be considered rather than cosine distance in this problem.

W2. Few (quantitative) experiments.
- This paper only provides a few experimental results, so I am not convinced that the proposed method is really useful and effective in practice. When is unsupervised noise synthesis useful?
- If the noise synthesis framework can be used as a data augmentation strategy, supervised/self-supervised training (for image classification) with the noise would be one evaluation metric.
- Why do high PSNR and SSIM values imply that the synthesized noises are realistic? They might be "easy-to-denoise" noises, not realistic ones.
- There is no ablation study, so I am not sure that whether each component is essential or not.
  - Without "perceptual loss", what happens? Also, do we need a "pre-trained" encoder for the perceptual loss? This requirement for the pre-trained encoder might be a weakness because the pre-trained encoder does not exist in some domains (e.g., medical images).
  - For MMD, how many samples do we need? Or, can we use the cosine distance?
- There is no comparison with supervised learning methods. The methods might be considered as an upper bound as self-supervised learning literature did.

---
### Editorial Comments
- Section 4.1., Baselines paragraph: ( Eq. 2) => (Eq. 2)
- Section 4.3., Empirical Results paragraph: the synthetic noise as . => I think something is missing
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper well incorporates the idea of contrastive learning into the noise synthesis problem. However, I am not convinced that the proposed method is really effective in practice because this paper only compares the proposed method with naive noise synthesis methods under a limited number of experimental settings.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4467 by Reviewer SqsX

content.title: Clarification on Weaknesses and Questions
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the time, feedback, and concrete comments that improve the quality of our work. Especially, the authors want to thank the encouraging comments from all reviewers, e.g. "**first work that uses UCL for noise synthesis**" [yC7E], "**novel**" [yC7E, SqsX ], "**well-written and easy to read**" [SqsX], and "**well incorporates the idea of contrastive learning into the noise synthesis problem**" [SqsX].

Sincerely, we try to address your concerns below and expect your feedback.

**Q**: Why MMD instead of cosine distance?  How many samples do we need for MMD?  
**A**: The state-of-the-art contrastive learning frameworks tend to use cosine similarity as they are comparing feature vectors in a Euclidean feature space. One significant difference between a standard feature vector and a noise tensor is that the first one **implicitly assumes an element-wise correspondence between two feature vectors**. But for noise tensors, we should not expect such correspondence as we are only interested in the distributional divergence. Note, we compute MMD between two noise tensors, For a tensor of shape 64 x 64 x 4, the sample number is 16384, which is **efficient to estimate the distributional divergence**.

This is explained in the last paragraph of Sec. 2:  
*Second, $\mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)$ requires that two feature vectors are projected into the same high-dimensional feature space, i.e. there will be an element-wise correspondence between two feature vectors.*


**Q**: When is unsupervised noise synthesis useful?  
**A**: The goal of this work is to present an alternative approach to statistical noise synthesis for the first time, as stated in Sec. 1. The existing studies on noise synthesis tend to rely on clean and noisy pairs to learn such a noise distribution. First, the proposed framework tries to **bridge the gap when paired data are not unavailable**. Second, CoNo could serve as a replacement when statistical noise synthesis can be used. Note, there is a trade-off when using CoNo, as explained in Sec. 4.4.


**Q**: Can be used as a data augmentation strategy?  
**A**: CoNo definitely could be used as a data augmentation strategy. However, as suggested in the title, the core contribution is to present a noise synthesis framework alternative to statistical methods. Thus, data augmentation is not the focus of this work, but this could be a future research direction. 


**Q**: Why do high PSNR and SSIM values imply that the synthesized noises are realistic?  
**A**: Note, although the denoiser is trained on the synthetic datasets, the evaluation is performed on the real datasets. We design this **proxy evaluation** protocol as it is difficult to directly evaluate the quantitative performance of synthetic noise when paired data is not available. The intuition here is that **when the training distribution (synthetic) and testing distribution (real) are similar, the denoising performance is good** (considering this as a domain adaptation problem if it helps). **A similar experimental design and phenomenon can be found in [1]**.  

[1] Abdelhamed et al., Noise flow: Noise modeling with conditional normalizing flows. ICCV 2019

**Q**: Without "perceptual loss", what happens? Also, do we need a "pre-trained" encoder for the perceptual loss?  
**A**: The perceptual loss plays a critical role in avoiding trivial solutions. Take an extreme example, a few overlapped pixels of two positive patches could have huge noise, which may change the regional semantic information. In addition to supervised pre-training, the encoder could be trained in a **self-supervised fashion**, e.g. [2, 3]. The same logic applies to the medical domain. In short, the encoder is to make the generated noisy image realistic by regularizing the representations in the feature space, while the feature space could have various choices. As the experiments are designed for common RGB images, we find that using an Imagenet pre-trained encoder is easy to implement and can achieve a reasonable performance under our experiment setting. We will clarify this in the revision.

[2] Chen et al. A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. ICML 2020   
[3] He et al. Momentum contrast for unsupervised visual representation learning. CVPR 2020

**Q**: There is no comparison with supervised learning methods.  
**A**: We agree that *the methods might be considered as an upper bound as self-supervised learning literature did*. However, the problem formulation of this work is that paired data are not available. Note, in our experimental setup, there are **only clean images** (Kodak dataset). The supervised learning methods are **not applicable** and thus omitted in the discussion.

content.title: Additional Comments to Author Response
content.comment:
I sincerely appreciate your efforts in the response, and I have read it in detail. In what follows, I describe my thoughts one by one.

**Q1. MMD.**
Thank you for the explanation. I get your point.

---

**Q2. When is unsupervised noise synthesis useful?**
I know this work is about statistical noise synthesis, and it does not use any noise information. So, my question was, when is the setup meaningful in practice? I'm not sure about importance of the motivation of this work.

---

**Q3. Can be used as a data augmentation strategy?**
Why is data augmentation not the focus of this work? If the synthesized noise is better (i.e., more realistic) than existing approaches, it should have several advantages in various scenarios. I think utilizing the noise as augmentation is a reasonable way to verify the advantage.

---

**Q4. Why do high PSNR and SSIM values imply that the synthesized noises are realistic?**
Thank you for the explanation. I get your point. However, I'm still not sure that the obtained gains (roughly +0.5 PSNR) are significant.

---

**Q5. Without "perceptual loss", what happens? Also, do we need a "pre-trained" encoder for the perceptual loss?**
In some domains, there exists no pre-trained encoder in both supervised and self-supervised fashions. My question was, can we start from scratch for the encoder? Also, I'm wondering about how much the contrastive loss is more important than the perceptual loss. For example, is learning without the contrastive loss (i.e., $\mathcal{L}_\text{perceptual}+\mathcal{L}_\text{alignment}$) not working? Such an ablation study seems to be necessary.

---

**Q6. There is no comparison with supervised learning methods.**
I know this paper's setup is unsupervised, so supervised learning methods are not applicable. Nevertheless, comparisons with the methods (using any supervised dataset) are meaningful because we can check whether the obtained gains are significant or not. Also, in Table 2, I find no comparison with AWGN- or NLF-pretrained models.

---

**Summary.** Overall, although some of my concerns are addressed, I'm still not convinced that this paper is well-motivated and empirically well-verified. I would like to keep my current rating.

content.title: Answers to Additional Questions
content.comment:
Thank you for improving the paper.

For the additional questions, the authors believe there are still misunderstandings that could be clarified. Though the score is final, the authors feel that it is necessary to answer the questions, for both completeness and clarity. 

**Q2**: *When is the setup meaningful in practice?*

**A**: Note, as stated in the paper, CoNo is just an alternative to statistical models. In current practical applications, statistical models are widely used in simulated experiments for low-level vision tasks. To the best of our knowledge, most low-level vision studies that focus on noisy images involve synthetic data generated by statistical models. CoNo could be a superior replacement.

**Q3**: *Why is data augmentation not the focus of this work?*  

**A**: As discussed in the original reply, we agree that data augmentation could be an interesting study for future work. Considering both the page limit and the coherency for the paper, we are unable to include the study of data augmentation in this version. As suggested by the reviewer, data augmentation could be a promising direction that requires extensive empirical analysis.

**Q4**: *I'm still not sure that the obtained gains (roughly +0.5 PSNR) are significant.*

**A**: We totally understand your concern. The quantitative results in proxy evaluation are only to validate the claim that CoNo is better than statistical models. This is different from direct evaluation where two models are trained end-to-end on the same task. Similar proxy evaluation protocols are commonly seen in high-level representation learning e.g. MoCo, SimCLR, BYOL. For this study, the claimed performance gain is meaningful.

**Q5.1**:  *Can we start from scratch for the encoder?* 

**A**: The encoder or the perceptual loss is a regularization term to make sure the generated noisy image and the clean image show similarity in the semantic feature space. This semantic feature space could be any meaningful feature space, even when the target domain is different from the source domain. For example, in RGB domain, ImageNet is already sufficient. 

**Q5.2**: *Also, I'm wondering about how much the contrastive loss is more important than the perceptual loss.*

**A**: Note, the contrastive loss plays a role in ensuring that the learning outcome fits Asm. 1, while the perceptual loss assures that the generated noisy images are realistic. Two losses are both important. Intuitively, with only the perceptual loss and the alignment loss suggested by the reviewer, the network could easily produce a trivial result that mimics AWGN, which is undesirable. We aim to uses the contrastive loss to fully leverage the flexibility (non-linearity) of Glow-based model.

**Q6.1**:  *Comparisons with the methods (using any supervised dataset) are meaningful.*

**A**: We politely emphasize that the purpose of this work is not self-supervised/unsupervised denoising. We infer from the reviewer's comment that the reviewer was talking about supervised learning for noise synthesis. This is indeed inapplicable. Using a different real noisy dataset could easily lead to unfair comparison (different data source, number of images). That is to say, we can not validate the significance of performance gain.

**Q6.2**: *In Table 2, I find no comparison with AWGN- or NLF-pretrained models.*

**A**: Thank you for the suggestion. We have shown that CoNo outperforms AWGN and NLF in Table 1. The purpose of Table 2 is to demonstrate that CoNo can be used in a real application.

Especially, the authors want to thank the encouraging comments from all reviewers, e.g. "**first work that uses UCL for noise synthesis**" [yC7E], "**novel**" [yC7E, SqsX ], "**well-written and easy to read**" [SqsX], and "**well incorporates the idea of contrastive learning into the noise synthesis problem**" [SqsX].

Sincerely, we try to address your concerns below and expect your feedback.

**Contributions**:  
* This is the first study of UCL / SSL on noise synthesis.
* We propose to use the signal-dependency of the synthetic noise as a discriminative feature in the instance discrimination pretext
task.
* We present an alternative noise synthesis framework to traditional statistical models when the noisy-and-clean image pairs are unavailable.

**Q**: It is hard to follow Section 3.3, maybe adding some examples or figures could help.  
**A**: Thank you for the suggestion. We have added Algorithm 1 to illustrate the batch-wise training for noise contrastive loss. Sec. 3.3 introduces the methodological contribution of *noise contrastive loss* and how to define positive and negative pairs in instance-wise discrimination. **We first discuss the motivations of using MMD as the distance function and then provide a mathematical derivation of MMD under our problem setting**. The workflow is depicted in Fig. 2.

**Q**: Why not using more training data to show the power of unsupervised training?  
**A**: First, we use Kodak, a well-known small dataset, to illustrate the effectiveness of CoNo. Second, as we use AWGN with different $\sigma$ and small random crops, there are already enough training samples considering there are almost unlimited combinations. Meanwhile, we only train the network to be sensitive to signal intensity and $\sigma$. This is different from standard large-scale training, where the images and labels are fixed. In our case, we can generate as many pairs of input noise tensor and image crop as needed. Third, using a small dataset makes the experiments controllable and easy to reproduce.

**Q**: From Fig.1 and Fig. 3, it is hard to tell which one of (c) and (d) is better? Maybe adding some explanations is better.  
**A**: Thank you for the suggestion. We have added explanations for Fig. 1. The qualitative explanations of Fig. 3 are described in Sec. 4.2.  
* *Note, although statistical models may describe photon noise, the real images have other noise sources (e.g. fixed-pattern noise,
defective pixels, clipped intensities, spatially correlated noise, amplification noise, and quantization
noise).*  
* *Moreover, statistical models such as AWGN and NLF tend to assume independence between the pixels. As a comparison, CoNo does not have this inductive bias. Meanwhile, the convolution operations give CoNo more flexibility in synthesizing the signal-dependent noise. **If we take a closer look at Fig. 3, CoNo generates noise with unnoticeable local patterns, which simulate the non-photon noise and
logically make the synthetic noisy images more similar to the real noisy images than rigid statistical models**. In our experiment, independent human viewers suggest that the noisy images synthesized by CoNo are **more perceptually comfortable** than the noisy images synthesized by AWGN and NLF under the same noise variance level. We hypothesize that this is due to the fact that the noisy images generated by CoNo share more similar characteristics with the commonly seen real noisy images, such as **intensity-based local patterns and pixel-wise dependence**.*

**Q**: Inconsistency between Assumption 1 and the definition of positive and negative pairs.  
**A**: Assumption 1 is based on empirical findings, which is also the motivation of this work. On average, Assumption 1 should hold but there could be failure cases. Think about a good **counter-example**,  there is a white circle in the center of a black paper. Apparently, the region within the white circle is drastically different from the black background, but they come from the same image. To avoid such extreme cases and stabilize the training process, we require two positive patches to overlap, i.e. enforce them to be similar. Following [1, 2], **the sampling process will not sample a negative pair from the same image**. In addition to training robustness, this sampling strategy also provides computational efficiency.  We have highlighted this in the revision.

[1] Chen et al. A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. ICML 2020  
[2] He et al. Momentum contrast for unsupervised visual representation learning. CVPR 2020

content.title: Answers to Additional Questions
content.comment:
Thank you for improving the paper. 

For the additional questions, the authors believe there are still misunderstandings that could be clarified. Though the score is final, the authors feel that it is necessary to answer the questions, for both completeness and clarity. 

**Q**: *The reviewer suggests using natural images (here, the authors infer that natural images are noisy).* 

**A**: We believe there still exists a misunderstanding around the problem formulation. Indeed, there are numerous noisy images without paired clean images, as mentioned by the reviewer. However, how to generate signal-dependent noise is the focus of this work. Note, paired (labeled) noisy and clean images are not always available. We focus on the situation that only clean images are avaialbel. Intuitively, it is more difficult to generate a synthetic clean image given a noisy image (this is the process of denoising) than generate a synthetic noisy image given a clean image. On the other hand, there are lots of clean images available for high-level vision tasks already. Thus, we believe that it is reasonable to study how to generate realistic noisy images given only clean images.

**Q**: *The reviewer suggests that given a labeled dataset, it is unnecessary for unsupervised training.*  

**A**: We respectfully disagree with this statement. Fundamentally, manually curating and annotating noisy images in low-level vision is difficult and time-consuming. Note, statistical noisy generation is still actively utilized in many vision tasks, which means labeled datasets are not always available.  The authors agree that when a labeled dataset is available, unsupervised training could be used to improve the supervised training, only when a labeled dataset is available. In our case, we present an alternative to statistical models. That is to say, as long as statistical models are still applied in vision tasks, so does CoNo.

replying_to: Replying to Unsupervised Contrastive Learning for Signal-Dependent Noise Synthesis

content.title: Summary of Revision
content.comment:
In addition to the rebuttal, the authors have revised the manuscript based on the reviewers' comments and suggestions.

1. We have added batch-wise training procedure (Algorithm 1) in Sec. 3.3 to illustrate the sampling and computing noise contrastive loss, suggested by Reviewer yC7E.
2. We have added explanations for Fig. 1, suggested by Reviewer yC7E.
3. We have clarified the definitions of positive pair and negative pair in Sec. 3.3, suggested by Reviewer yC7E.
4. We have fixed the typos and further proofread the paper, suggested by Reviewer SqsX.

Meanwhile, because there are still uncertainties of the initial reviews, the authors will wait for further actions of SACs and the AC, and keep this summary of revision open until the end of the discussion period.

**Import Update**  on Nov. 22  
In the newest version of revision, we provide **strong evidence** that CoNo shows advantages over AWGN and NLF, in *Analysis of Noise Distribution* and Fig. 5. We further study the relationship between the pixel intensity and noise to show that CoNo can better model the physical noise than AWGN and NLF.
